Performing initial audit of PKGBUILD to ensure that we can safely run `makepkg`
LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD contains only standard variable assignments and function definitions at the top level. Running `makepkg --printsrcinfo` sources the PKGBUILD and evaluates only the global scope — it does not execute `package()`, `build()`, `prepare()`, or `pkgver()`. All top-level entries are benign: standard metadata variables (`pkgname`, `pkgver`, `pkgdesc`, etc.), a `source` array, a `sha256sums` array (both with actual checksums, not SKIP), a `DLAGENTS` definition (which stores a download handler string but does not execute during sourcing), and a `package()` function definition. No command substitutions, network requests, or data exfiltration occur at the global scope during `--printsrcinfo`.
</details>
<evidence>
</evidence>
<summary>Safe: no executable code at top-level scope during printsrcinfo.</summary>
</security_assessment>

+ Initial PKGBUILD audit complete -- Safe: no executable code at top-level scope during printsrcinfo.

LLM auditresponse for download_foundry.bash:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This script is a standard AUR download helper for FoundryVTT. It authenticates against foundryvtt.com using CSRF tokens, downloads the specified version, and optionally stores credentials in the system secret service via `secret-tool`. All network requests go to the legitimate upstream domain (foundryvtt.com). No obfuscated code, eval, base64, or suspicious downloads are present. The only minor concern is that the password appears in curl's command-line arguments (visible via `ps`), which is an inherent limitation of this pattern used by many AUR helpers, but not evidence of malice. The cookie jar is stored in a temp file and cleaned up at exit. Input is validated against an expected version pattern before processing.
</details>
<evidence>
